title: Rewrite a cold outreach email
promptText:
You are a B2B sales expert who specializes in writing concise, buyer-centric outbound emails.

Rewrite the following cold email so that it:
- Opens with a specific, relevant observation about {{prospect_company}} (use what I provide, do not fabricate)
- Focuses on one business problem, not a list of features
- Has a single, low-friction call to action (a question or a short calendar link ask)
- Stays under 120 words in the body
- Sounds like a human wrote it on a Tuesday morning, not a template

Original email:
{{original_email}}

Context about the prospect:
- Company: {{prospect_company}}
- Role/title of recipient: {{recipient_title}}
- Known pain point or trigger event: {{trigger_event}}

Output: the rewritten email only — subject line, then body. No commentary.
use_when: You have a draft cold email that feels generic or too long and want a sharper, more personalized version before sending.
anti_pattern: Do not use this to generate cold emails from scratch with no prospect research — the output will be as generic as the input.

title: Build a discovery call prep brief
use_when: You have a scheduled discovery call in the next 24 hours and want to walk in with a focused plan rather than a generic question list.
anti_pattern: Do not skip filling in known context — a blank {{known_context}} produces shallow questions that waste the prospect's time.

title: Map objections to handling responses
use_when: You are building deal coaching material, preparing a rep for a tough conversation, or debriefing a stalled deal.
anti_pattern: Do not treat objections as scripts to memorize — use these as starting points that reps adapt to each conversation.

title: Summarize CRM notes into a deal brief
use_when: You need to quickly onboard a manager or colleague to a deal's status, or prepare a pipeline review without re-reading every activity log.
anti_pattern: Do not paste notes that contain customer PII or confidential contract terms into a non-enterprise AI tool.

title: Draft a proposal outline from a brief
use_when: You are kicking off a formal proposal and want a structure aligned to the customer's stated priorities before writing begins.
anti_pattern: Do not use this outline as the final proposal — a skeleton without the customer's own words and specific evidence rarely wins.

title: Generate win/loss interview questions
use_when: You are scheduling a post-decision debrief with a buyer and need questions that surface honest, actionable intelligence rather than polite feedback.
anti_pattern: Do not conduct a win/loss interview with the rep who owned the deal in the room — their presence biases the customer's answers.

title: Prepare a deal review brief for leadership
use_when: A deal is in late stage and you need a crisp, leadership-ready summary before a pipeline review meeting.
anti_pattern: Do not soften the risk assessment to look optimistic — leadership needs accurate information, not comfort.

title: Write a champion coaching email
use_when: Your champion needs to sell the deal internally and you want to arm them with talking points without putting them in an awkward position.
anti_pattern: Do not make this email read like a vendor briefing — it should feel like two colleagues coordinating, not a sales tactic.

title: Rewrite a support reply with empathy
promptText:
You are a customer experience editor reviewing support replies before they are sent.

Rewrite the following draft support reply so that it:
1. Opens by acknowledging the customer's frustration or situation in one genuine sentence (no 'I apologize for the inconvenience')
2. States clearly what you are doing or what happened
3. Provides the resolution or next step in plain, numbered steps if there is more than one action
4. Closes warmly without being sycophantic

Constraints:
- Do not add hollow phrases ('I totally understand', 'That's a great question')
- Do not make promises about timelines unless they are already in the draft
- Keep the reply under 150 words unless technical detail requires more
- Match the register of the customer's message: if they were professional, be professional; if casual, be human

Draft reply:
{{draft_reply}}

Customer message (for context):
{{customer_message}}

Output the rewritten reply only.
use_when: A support rep's draft reply is technically correct but reads as cold, defensive, or overly formal for the situation.
anti_pattern: Do not over-empathize to the point of removing factual content — empathy without resolution does not help the customer.

title: Assess escalation risk in a support ticket
promptText:
You are a support quality analyst. Review the following support ticket thread and assess escalation risk.

Ticket content:
{{ticket_thread}}

Customer context (if known):
- Account tier: {{account_tier}}
- Days since original submission: {{days_open}}
- Number of previous tickets in last 90 days: {{prior_ticket_count}}

Provide:
1. Escalation risk: Low / Medium / High — with one sentence of reasoning
2. Sentiment trajectory: Getting better / Stable / Deteriorating
3. Unaddressed issue(s): list any customer concern not yet responded to in the thread
4. Recommended action: specific next step (e.g., 'assign to senior agent', 'proactive outreach from CSM', 'resolve within 4 hours')
5. Suggested opening line if a human follows up

Be direct. Do not hedge excessively.
use_when: A ticket is getting long, the customer seems frustrated, or a manager wants a fast second opinion before deciding whether to escalate.
anti_pattern: Do not use this to replace human judgment on sensitive legal or compliance complaints — those require a specialist review.

title: Draft a KB article from a ticket cluster
promptText:
You are a technical writer who turns support ticket patterns into clear knowledge base articles.

I am providing a set of support tickets about the same issue. Write a KB article that will deflect this ticket type in the future.

Ticket summaries:
{{ticket_summaries}}

Product area: {{product_area}}
Audience: {{audience_description}}

Structure the article as:
1. Title (plain language, starts with a verb or a question the user would search)
2. Problem description (2–3 sentences — describe the symptom, not the cause)
3. Cause (optional, 1–2 sentences — only include if it helps the user)
4. Solution (numbered steps, imperative mood, one action per step)
5. If it still does not work (2–3 bullets for common variations or follow-up steps)
6. Related articles (3 placeholder titles)

Constraints: no jargon without definition, active voice throughout, steps should be completable by {{audience_description}}.
use_when: Three or more tickets have come in for the same issue and you want to write a self-serve article before the next wave hits.
anti_pattern: Do not publish the article without a product SME reviewing the solution steps — ticket patterns show symptoms, not always root causes.

title: Rewrite a macro to match customer tone
promptText:
You are a support quality specialist. Rewrite the following canned response (macro) into three tone variants:

Original macro:
{{original_macro}}

Context:
- Issue type: {{issue_type}}
- Product: {{product_name}}

Variant 1 — Formal/Professional: appropriate for enterprise or B2B customers who write formally.
Variant 2 — Friendly/Conversational: appropriate for a consumer product or a customer who wrote casually.
Variant 3 — Urgent/Empathetic: appropriate when the customer is clearly frustrated or has been waiting.

For each variant:
- Keep the same core information as the original
- Adjust opening, word choice, and closing
- Do not add information not in the original unless clearly labeled as a placeholder
- Stay under 120 words per variant

Output: all three variants labeled clearly.
use_when: Your team uses macros but the one-size tone is causing mismatches with different customer personas or emotional states.
anti_pattern: Do not replace all macros with tone variants — only do this for high-volume ticket types where tone genuinely affects satisfaction.

title: Analyze a CSAT decline and draft a team memo
use_when: CSAT has dropped measurably and you need a fast, honest analysis before a team meeting or leadership update.
anti_pattern: Do not skip qualitative review of actual tickets — CSAT numbers and verbatims alone may miss the real pattern.

title: Draft a proactive SLA breach notification
use_when: A ticket is approaching or has crossed an SLA deadline and you want to reach out before the customer does.
anti_pattern: Do not send this message without verifying the ETA with the engineering or ops team first — committing to a wrong deadline compounds the breach.

title: Scrub a job description for biased language
promptText:
You are a talent acquisition specialist trained in inclusive hiring practices.

Review the following job description and:
1. Identify words or phrases that research shows skew the applicant pool (e.g., gendered adjectives, requirement inflation, culture-fit language, ageist phrasing)
2. Suggest a neutral replacement for each flagged item
3. Flag any 'nice to have' requirements that are listed as 'required' — these may be filtering out qualified candidates
4. Rewrite the 'About the role' and 'What you will do' sections using inclusive language

Job description:
{{job_description}}

Role level: {{role_level}}
Department: {{department}}

Output format:
- Flagged items table: Original phrase | Issue | Suggested replacement
- Rewritten sections (clearly labeled)
- 2–3 sentence summary of overall inclusivity assessment

Do not change the actual requirements — only the language used to describe them.
use_when: You have a draft JD and want a structured review before posting to reduce unintentional applicant pool narrowing.
anti_pattern: Do not treat this as a complete DEI audit — language is one lever; sourcing strategy and interview process matter equally.

title: Generate structured interview questions by competency
promptText:
You are a talent acquisition specialist experienced in structured, competency-based interviewing.

Generate a structured interview question set for the following role:
- Role: {{role_title}}
- Level: {{role_level}}
- Key competencies to assess: {{competency_list}}
- Interview type: {{interview_type}} (e.g., behavioral, technical screen, case, executive)

For each competency, write:
1. One behavioral question (STAR-format eliciting: past situation, action, result)
2. One follow-up probe question
3. What a strong answer looks like (2–3 bullet points)
4. A red flag to listen for (1 bullet)

Constraints:
- Questions must be legally compliant for {{jurisdiction}} (avoid protected-class topics)
- No leading questions
- Each question answerable in 3–5 minutes
- Behavioral questions should use 'Tell me about a time...' or 'Describe a situation where...'

Output as a structured guide the interviewer can print and use.
use_when: You are building or refreshing an interview guide and want questions that consistently reveal relevant signals across all candidates.
anti_pattern: Do not use the same question set for all roles — tailor it even if only one competency changes between similar roles.

title: Build a 30-60-90 day onboarding plan
use_when: A new hire is starting within two weeks and the manager needs a structured, role-specific plan rather than a generic checklist.
anti_pattern: Do not treat the 30-60-90 as fixed — review it at each milestone and update based on what you have actually learned.

title: Scaffold a performance review draft
use_when: You have gathered all your notes and feedback but need help structuring it into a coherent, fair, legally defensible review draft.
anti_pattern: Do not rely on this draft without reading it carefully — AI cannot know nuance that only you observed in the working relationship.

title: Tone-check an internal HR communication
promptText:
You are an internal communications specialist with experience in HR messaging.

Review the following HR communication draft and assess its tone and effectiveness:

Draft:
{{draft_communication}}

Context:
- Audience: {{audience}}
- Topic sensitivity: {{sensitivity_level}} (e.g., policy change, layoff, compensation update, culture initiative)
- Intended reaction: {{intended_reaction}}

Provide:
1. Tone assessment: how will this land? (3–4 sentences, be honest)
2. Flagged phrases: list any sentences likely to cause confusion, anxiety, or cynicism, with brief reasoning
3. Structural gaps: is there a missing section (e.g., no FAQ, no 'what happens next', no named contact)?
4. Revised version of the most problematic paragraph
5. One-line overall verdict: 'Ready to send', 'Send with minor edits', or 'Needs significant revision'

Be direct. HR communications that obscure information erode trust.
use_when: You have a draft of a sensitive HR communication and want an honest read before it goes to employees.
anti_pattern: Do not use this to soften a message that should be direct — employees can usually tell when something is being obscured.

title: Generate offer conversation talking points
use_when: A recruiter or manager is about to deliver a verbal offer and wants to feel prepared for the conversation rather than improvising.
anti_pattern: Do not use these talking points to pressure a candidate — the goal is to inform and invite, not manipulate.

title: Prepare exit interview questions
promptText:
You are an HR business partner conducting an exit interview. Generate a structured question guide.

Employee context:
- Role: {{role_title}}
- Department: {{department}}
- Tenure: {{tenure}}
- Departure type: {{departure_type}} (voluntary / involuntary / retirement)
- Known reason for leaving (if any): {{known_reason}}

Generate 10 questions in 4 groups:
1. Decision to leave (3 questions): when the decision was made, contributing factors, tipping point
2. Experience at the company (3 questions): what worked well, what they would change, team dynamics
3. Role-specific factors (2 questions): support, clarity, growth opportunity
4. Improvements and recommendations (2 questions): one thing we should stop doing, one we should start

For each question: the question itself, why we ask it (internal note only), and what a useful answer sounds like.

Note: if departure type is involuntary, limit questions to experience and improvements only — do not ask about the decision to leave.
use_when: You are scheduling an exit interview and want questions that generate actionable retention intelligence rather than polite generic feedback.
anti_pattern: Do not conduct exit interviews in a way that feels like data harvesting — the tone should be genuinely curious and non-defensive.

title: Rewrite a policy document in plain language
promptText:
You are a workplace communications specialist who makes policy documents readable by normal humans.

Rewrite the following policy section in plain language suitable for all employees, including those who are not native English speakers or who do not have a legal background.

Original policy text:
{{policy_text}}

Policy type: {{policy_type}}
Audience: all employees

Rewrite guidelines:
- Use second person ('you') throughout
- Replace legal or HR jargon with everyday words (table at end with original vs. replacement terms)
- Use numbered lists for processes, bullet lists for options
- Maximum sentence length: 25 words
- Include a 'What this means for you' summary box at the start (3 bullets, plain language)
- Preserve all legal requirements — do not simplify away anything that changes the meaning

Output: plain-language version + jargon replacement table.
use_when: An HR policy reads like a legal contract and employees either ignore it or need a lawyer to understand it.
anti_pattern: Do not finalize the plain-language version without legal review — simplifying language must not alter legal obligations.

title: Summarize a meeting into a structured action log
promptText:
You are a chief of staff helping a manager follow through on meeting outcomes.

Convert the following meeting notes or transcript into a structured summary:

Raw notes or transcript:
{{meeting_notes}}

Meeting context:
- Meeting name: {{meeting_name}}
- Date: {{meeting_date}}
- Attendees: {{attendee_list}}

Produce:
1. One-sentence meeting objective and whether it was achieved
2. Key decisions made (bullet list — decisions only, not discussions)
3. Action items table: Action | Owner | Due date | Dependencies
4. Open questions not resolved (bullet list)
5. What the manager should do in the next 24 hours (1–3 specific items)

Do not include discussion threads that did not result in a decision or action. Strip filler. Be specific.
use_when: After a meeting with multiple decisions and owners, you need a clean record that actually drives follow-through.
anti_pattern: Do not send this summary to participants without reviewing it — transcription errors or misattributions need a human check.

title: Run a decision pre-mortem
use_when: You are about to make or recommend a significant decision and want structured adversarial thinking before you commit.
anti_pattern: Do not use a pre-mortem to endlessly delay a decision — set a deadline for the analysis and honor it.

title: Draft working norms for a new team
promptText:
You are an organizational effectiveness consultant. Help a manager draft a working norms document for a team.

Team context:
- Team size: {{team_size}}
- Work model: {{work_model}} (e.g., remote-first, hybrid 2 days, fully on-site)
- Team function: {{team_function}}
- Common friction points the manager wants to address: {{friction_points}}
- Values the manager wants to reinforce: {{values}}

Draft working norms in these categories:
1. Communication (response times, channels, async vs. sync)
2. Meetings (standing meetings, prep expectations, no-meeting windows)
3. Decision-making (who decides what, how disagreements are handled)
4. Deep work (focus time, interruption norms)
5. Feedback and recognition (how we give feedback, how we celebrate)

For each norm: write it as a positive, active statement ('We do X') not a rule ('Do not do Y'). Include the reasoning in one sentence per norm so the team understands the why.

Total: 12–18 norms. Flag 3 as 'team to ratify together' to encourage co-ownership.
use_when: A new team is forming or an existing team needs to reset its working agreement after a structural or personnel change.
anti_pattern: Do not impose norms without team input — draft them, then run a session where the team amends and commits to them.

title: Prepare skip-level meeting questions
promptText:
You are an experienced people leader preparing for skip-level 1:1 meetings with employees who report to your direct reports.

Context:
- Your role: {{your_role}}
- Employee role: {{employee_role}}
- Their manager: {{manager_name}}
- Relationship history: {{relationship_history}} (e.g., first skip-level, quarterly check-in, post-reorg)
- Any context you have about current team climate: {{team_climate}}

Generate:
1. Three opening questions that signal you are there to listen, not audit their manager
2. Three questions about the employee's work experience, growth, and clarity on direction
3. Two questions that surface potential team-level issues without putting the employee in a difficult position
4. One closing question that invites the employee to ask you something

For each question: a brief note on what you are listening for.

Constraints: no questions that ask employees to evaluate their manager by name. Frame around the employee's experience, not the manager's performance.
use_when: You are preparing for skip-level 1:1s and want questions that build trust and surface signal without damaging the manager-employee relationship.
anti_pattern: Do not share your skip-level notes with the employee's direct manager without the employee's knowledge — that breaks trust quickly.

title: Prepare to deliver difficult feedback
use_when: You are preparing for a feedback conversation that you have been avoiding, or that feels high-stakes and you want to walk in with structure.
anti_pattern: Do not script every word — use this to prepare your thinking, then have the conversation naturally.

title: Build a standing 1:1 agenda structure
promptText:
You are a management coach. Help me design a standing 1:1 agenda for a direct report.

Context:
- Direct report role: {{direct_report_role}}
- Meeting cadence: {{meeting_cadence}} (e.g., weekly 30 min, biweekly 45 min)
- Current focus areas: {{current_priorities}}
- What I know about what motivates this person: {{motivation_context}}
- Any current challenges or tensions: {{current_challenges}}

Design a standing agenda template with:
1. A rotating opening question (give me 5 options that vary: mood check / priority check / energy check)
2. Employee-first section (15 min): their updates, blocks, and asks — no manager agenda
3. Manager section (10 min if 30-min meeting): one topic I need to cover, no more
4. Growth/development question (2 min): a rotating prompt to discuss once per month
5. Closing: what does success look like before we meet again?

Also write 3 'override prompts' — questions to drop the agenda for in specific situations (performance concern, major win, something seems off).
use_when: You want to stop improvising 1:1s and have a consistent structure that puts the employee first without being rigid.
anti_pattern: Do not run through the agenda as a checklist — it is a structure to fall back on, not a script to follow.

title: Draft a project kickoff brief
use_when: A new project is starting and you need a shared document that aligns the team on goals, roles, and constraints before work begins.
anti_pattern: Do not treat the kickoff brief as a contract — it is a starting alignment document that should be updated as the project evolves.

title: Draft a performance improvement plan outline
use_when: A manager and HRBP are ready to formalize a performance improvement process and need a starting structure that is specific and legally grounded.
anti_pattern: Do not use a PIP as a documentation trail to fire someone you have already decided to let go — that creates legal liability and destroys trust.

title: Sharpen a product positioning statement
use_when: Your current positioning feels generic, is not differentiating from competitors, or has not been revisited since the product evolved.
anti_pattern: Do not finalize positioning based on this output alone — test the top option in customer conversations before it goes into materials.

title: Generate headline A/B test variants
promptText:
You are a direct-response copywriter who specializes in headlines that drive click-through and conversions.

Context:
- Product or offer: {{product_or_offer}}
- Landing page goal: {{conversion_goal}}
- Target audience: {{target_audience}}
- Current headline: {{current_headline}}
- Current conversion rate (if known): {{current_cr}}

Generate 8 headline variants grouped by approach:
1. Benefit-first (2 variants): lead with the specific outcome
2. Problem-first (2 variants): name the pain before the solution
3. Curiosity or contrarian (2 variants): challenge a belief or create a question
4. Social proof (2 variants): anchor to evidence or adoption

For each variant:
- The headline (under 12 words)
- A subheadline that supports it (under 20 words)
- The psychological lever it pulls
- The audience segment it is most likely to resonate with

Flag the two you would test first and why.
use_when: Your landing page headline is underperforming and you want a structured set of test variants grounded in different copywriting frameworks.
anti_pattern: Do not run all 8 variants simultaneously — pick 1–2 to test at a time so you accumulate clean learnings.

title: Build a customer persona from behavioral data
use_when: You have a useful segment in your CRM but no structured persona, and you want one that is grounded in real data rather than assumptions.
anti_pattern: Do not create a persona without real data inputs — a persona built on assumptions reinforces existing biases rather than challenging them.

title: Draft a product launch email sequence
use_when: You are launching a new product or major feature and need a sequenced email campaign that builds momentum without burning out your list.
anti_pattern: Do not send all four emails to your entire list — segment by relevance and suppress recent purchasers or uninvolved segments.

title: Outline a customer case study
use_when: You have a strong customer result and an approval to write it up, and you want a structured outline to brief a writer or approach the customer interview.
anti_pattern: Do not publish a case study without final customer approval on all quotes and specific metrics — legal and PR risk is real.

title: Build a competitive battle card
use_when: A competitor is showing up regularly in your deals and your reps need a factual, usable resource — not a marketing brochure.
anti_pattern: Do not base a battle card on assumptions or your own marketing materials — use actual competitive intelligence and update it quarterly.

title: Generate a pull request description
promptText:
You are a software engineer writing a clear, reviewer-friendly pull request description.

PR context:
- What this PR does (brief): {{pr_summary}}
- Ticket or issue link: {{ticket_link}}
- Type of change: {{change_type}} (e.g., bug fix, feature, refactor, dependency update, hotfix)
- Files changed (list key ones): {{key_files}}
- Testing done: {{testing_done}}
- Any deployment notes or flags: {{deployment_notes}}

Write a PR description with these sections:
## What
(2–4 sentences: the change in plain language, what problem it solves)

## Why
(2–3 sentences: the motivation — link to ticket if helpful)

## How
(bullet list: the approach taken and any significant decisions made)

## Testing
(bullet list: what was tested, how, and what edge cases were considered)

## Deployment / Rollout Notes
(any flags, config changes, migration steps, or rollback considerations)

## Screenshots (if UI change)
(placeholder — note what screenshots to attach)

Do not include secrets, tokens, or internal usernames in the description.
use_when: You have finished a change and want a structured PR description that gives reviewers context without making them read the entire diff first.
anti_pattern: Do not skip the 'Why' section — reviewers need to understand intent to judge whether the implementation is correct.

title: Generate a code review checklist for a feature
promptText:
You are a senior software engineer building a code review checklist for a specific type of change.

Change context:
- Feature or area: {{feature_description}}
- Language/framework: {{language_framework}}
- Risk level: {{risk_level}} (low / medium / high — e.g., payment path = high)
- Reviewer expertise level: {{reviewer_level}} (junior / mid / senior)

Generate a layered code review checklist organized into:
1. Correctness (does it do what it says?): 4–6 questions
2. Readability and maintainability: 3–5 questions
3. Performance: 2–4 questions (calibrated to risk level — do not over-engineer for low-risk changes)
4. Security: 3–5 questions, scaled to risk level
5. Testing: 3–4 questions
6. Deployment and operations: 2–3 questions

For high-risk changes, add a section:
7. Escalation triggers: conditions under which the reviewer should block merge and escalate

Each item should be a yes/no question or an imperative ('Verify that...'), not a vague instruction.
use_when: Your team's code review process is inconsistent and you want a repeatable checklist that raises the floor without slowing reviewers down.
anti_pattern: Do not apply a one-size checklist to all changes — a two-line config fix and a new payment flow need different levels of scrutiny.

title: Summarize an incident timeline for a postmortem
use_when: An incident has been resolved and you need to rapidly compile a coherent timeline from fragmented chat logs, alerts, and notes before the postmortem.
anti_pattern: Do not treat this summary as the complete postmortem — it is the input to the investigation, not the output.

title: Draft an RFC outline for a technical proposal
use_when: You are proposing a meaningful technical change and need a structured document that invites good feedback before implementation begins.
anti_pattern: Do not write an RFC for changes that are clearly the right approach with no real alternatives — an RFC is for decisions with genuine trade-offs.

title: Prioritize a technical debt backlog
promptText:
You are a senior engineering manager helping a team prioritize its technical debt backlog.

Debt items:
{{debt_backlog}}

Context:
- Team size: {{team_size}}
- Upcoming product commitments (next 90 days): {{product_commitments}}
- Known reliability or security issues: {{reliability_concerns}}
- Business growth trajectory: {{growth_context}}

For each debt item, assess:
1. Impact if not addressed (High / Medium / Low) with one-sentence reasoning
2. Effort to address (T-shirt size: S / M / L / XL)
3. Urgency (Urgent / Normal / Backlog)
4. Dependency risk: does this block or slow other work?

Then produce:
- A prioritized top-5 list with brief rationale for each ranking
- One item that could be addressed in a single sprint with high impact
- One item to defer and why
- A recommendation for how much of the next quarter to allocate to debt vs. features (expressed as a percentage)

Be honest about trade-offs. Technical debt is a legitimate business concern, not just a team preference.
use_when: Your team has a growing debt backlog and needs a structured way to communicate trade-offs to product and business stakeholders.
anti_pattern: Do not use this prioritization to avoid product work indefinitely — the goal is sustainable pace, not perfect code.

title: Draft an on-call runbook for a service
promptText:
You are a reliability engineer writing an on-call runbook for an engineering service.

Service context:
- Service name: {{service_name}}
- What it does: {{service_description}}
- Owner team: {{owner_team}}
- Key dependencies: {{dependencies}}
- Common alert types: {{common_alerts}}
- Known failure modes: {{failure_modes}}

Write a runbook template with these sections:
1. Service overview (3–5 sentences: purpose, criticality, business impact if down)
2. Architecture quick reference (bullet list of key components and their roles)
3. Alert response guide: for each alert in {{common_alerts}}, provide:
   - What it means
   - First diagnostic step
   - Common resolution
   - Escalation path if not resolved in 15 min
4. Diagnostic commands (placeholder table: Command | What it checks | Expected output vs. abnormal)
5. Escalation contacts (placeholder table)
6. Rollback procedure (numbered steps, generic — fill in actual commands)
7. Post-incident checklist

This is a template structure — the team fills in the actual commands and contacts.
use_when: A service lacks a runbook and engineers are on-call without a structured guide for the most common failure scenarios.
anti_pattern: Do not publish a runbook without a live walkthrough with the team — a runbook no one has practiced is barely better than none.

title: Stress-test a board update narrative
promptText:
You are an experienced board director reviewing a company update before it is presented.

Board update draft:
{{board_update_draft}}

Company context:
- Stage: {{company_stage}}
- Key metrics this period: {{key_metrics}}
- Major decisions being asked of the board: {{board_asks}}

Review the narrative and provide:
1. Clarity check: are there any claims that are vague, unsupported, or that a director would immediately question?
2. Logic gaps: does the narrative connect the data to the conclusions? Where does the logic break?
3. Missing context: what does a board member need to know that is not in this draft?
4. The 3 questions a critical board member will ask during the presentation
5. A suggested revision for the executive summary — tighter, more direct, acknowledges challenges without spinning them

Tone: honest, board-level. Do not sugarcoat weaknesses in the draft.
use_when: You are finalizing a board deck and want an adversarial read that surfaces the questions you will get before you are in the room.
anti_pattern: Do not use this review to remove all difficult information — boards lose trust when bad news is buried or minimized.

title: Edit an all-hands script for clarity and impact
promptText:
You are an executive communications coach. Review and edit the following all-hands script for a company meeting.

Script draft:
{{script_draft}}

Context:
- Company size: {{company_size}}
- Meeting type: {{meeting_type}} (e.g., quarterly all-hands, post-announcement, crisis communication)
- Key message the CEO wants employees to leave with: {{key_message}}
- Current employee mood/concerns (if known): {{employee_concerns}}

Provide:
1. Opening assessment: does the script open with energy and purpose? If not, rewrite the first 60 seconds.
2. Message clarity: is the key message {{key_message}} clearly stated and memorable? Where does it land?
3. Emotional tone: does the script acknowledge what employees are feeling before moving to what leadership wants to say?
4. Credibility risks: any phrases that sound corporate, evasive, or that will generate eye-rolls
5. Revised version of the most problematic section
6. Suggested interactive element or question to include to avoid a one-way broadcast feeling

Do not rewrite the entire script — focus on the sections that most need attention.
use_when: A leadership team is preparing for an all-hands that addresses something significant (a change, a challenging period, or a major announcement).
anti_pattern: Do not over-produce an all-hands script to the point where the speaker sounds rehearsed and inauthentic — some natural variation is good.

title: Write a decision memo for leadership
use_when: You need to bring a decision to leadership with a structured case rather than walking through it verbally in a meeting without preparation.
anti_pattern: Do not write a decision memo for decisions that are already made — use it for genuine choices where leadership input is needed.

title: Plan your week on Monday morning
use_when: You are starting a week that feels busy and unclear, and you want a structured way to prioritize before reacting to your inbox.
anti_pattern: Do not over-plan — a plan with 20 items is not a plan, it is a wish list. Keep this list to things that actually matter this week.

title: Run a structured weekly review
use_when: It is Friday afternoon or Monday morning and you want to close the loop on the week rather than just rolling into the next one.
anti_pattern: Do not turn the weekly review into a guilt session — the goal is insight and intention, not a performance report.

title: Rewrite technical content for a smart non-expert
promptText:
You are a skilled explainer who can take dense, technical content and make it clear to a smart person who is not a specialist in this field.

Original content:
{{original_content}}

Context:
- Original audience (specialists): {{original_audience}}
- New target audience: {{target_audience}}
- Purpose of the explanation: {{explanation_purpose}}

Rewrite the content so that:
1. Every piece of jargon is either eliminated or briefly defined on first use
2. Complex ideas are anchored to an analogy or concrete example the target audience would recognize
3. The 'so what' — why this matters — is clear within the first paragraph
4. Any precision lost in simplification is explicitly noted ('this is a simplification; the full detail is...')
5. Length is reduced to what is necessary for the target audience's purpose

Do not dumb it down — aim for clarity, not simplicity. The audience is intelligent, just not expert in this domain.
use_when: You have a technical document, analysis, or explanation that needs to be shared with an audience who does not have the background to follow the original.
anti_pattern: Do not strip out so much nuance that the explanation becomes misleading — clarity and accuracy must coexist.

title: Draft a post-purchase onboarding message sequence
use_when: You are setting up or refreshing a post-purchase onboarding sequence and want drafts grounded in product reality, not generic welcome emails.
anti_pattern: Do not send all three messages on day one — spacing matters more than volume for early customer experience.

title: Triage and categorize a batch of support tickets
promptText:
You are a support operations analyst. Review the following batch of support ticket summaries and categorize each one for routing and prioritization.

Ticket batch:
{{ticket_batch}}

Product context:
- Product name: {{product_name}}
- Support tiers: {{support_tiers}} (e.g., Tier 1: billing/account, Tier 2: technical, Tier 3: engineering escalation)
- Current team capacity: {{team_capacity}}

For each ticket produce a one-row entry in a table:
Ticket ID | Category | Priority (P1–P4) | Recommended tier | Key reason | Suggested owner type

Priority definitions:
- P1: Customer is blocked from core functionality
- P2: Significant degradation, workaround exists
- P3: Non-urgent functional issue or question
- P4: Feature request, low urgency

After the table, provide:
1. Volume by category (summary)
2. Any tickets that appear to be duplicates
3. The single highest-priority action for the support lead right now

Do not guess at technical causes — categorize based on the symptom described.
use_when: You have a queue backlog or a morning ticket pile and need a structured way to route and prioritize before the team starts working.
anti_pattern: Do not use this categorization as the final routing decision without a human reviewing P1 tickets — AI can misread urgency signals.
